title: Animal Body Groups
keyIdea: Animals with backbones are sorted into five groups by their bodies, not by where they live. Mammals have fur or hair and feed their babies milk. Birds have feathers, a beak and wings. Fish have fins and gills, and most have scales. Reptiles have dry, scaly skin. Amphibians, like frogs, have smooth, damp skin.

kid: Look at what covers an animal. A bear has fur. An owl has feathers. A fish has scales. A snake has scales too, but they are dry. A frog has smooth, damp skin.

We sort animals into groups by their bodies. Mammals have fur or hair, and their babies drink milk. Birds have feathers, a beak and wings. Fish have fins and gills. Reptiles have dry scales. Amphibians have smooth, damp skin.
Some animals are tricky. A whale lives in the sea, but it is not a fish. It breathes air and its babies drink milk, so it is a mammal. A bat can fly, but it has fur. It is a mammal too.
A penguin cannot fly, but it has feathers and a beak. So it is a bird. Where an animal lives does not tell you its group. Its body does.
adult: The English national curriculum asks Year 1 pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals' and to 'describe and compare the structure of a variety of common animals'. In the US, NGSS 1-LS1-1 asks children to use what they notice about the external parts of animals, such as fins, feathers and shells. These five groups are all vertebrates, animals with a backbone.

Each group is defined by its body. Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk. Birds have feathers, a beak, two wings and two legs, and lay hard-shelled eggs. Fish live in water, breathe with gills and have fins, and most are covered in scales. Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and breathe air. Amphibians, such as frogs, toads and newts, have smooth, damp skin and usually begin life in water as tadpoles.

Common mistakes: sorting by habitat or movement, so a whale or a dolphin becomes a fish and a bat becomes a bird; thinking all birds fly, then rejecting the penguin or the ostrich; muddling reptiles and amphibians, because a lizard and a newt look alike; thinking a snake is slimy when its scales are dry; and calling every small creature an animal group of its own. Ask 'what covers its body?' and 'how do its babies feed?' rather than 'where does it live?'.

In the lab your child matches animals to their coverings, sorts eight animals (including the whale, the bat and the penguin) into the five groups, builds a bird, a fish and a mammal from body parts, finds the odd one out, and chooses the clue that tells a shark from a dolphin.

familyTip: On a walk or with a picture book, play 'fur, feathers, scales or skin?'. Point at an animal and ask what covers it, then which group that puts it in. Try a tricky one: a duck swims, but is it a fish?

visual.caption: Which group is each animal in? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match coverings, sort animals into five groups, build an animal, find the odd one out, tell look-alikes apart.

practice.prompt: In a field there are {a} rabbits and {b} crows. How many of them are birds?
practice.hint: Rabbits have fur. Crows have feathers and a beak. Which ones are birds?
practice.explain: The {b} crows have feathers, so they are birds. The {a} rabbits have fur: they are mammals. The answer is {b}.

practice.prompt: A pond has {a} frogs and {b} fish. How many of them are amphibians?
practice.hint: Frogs have smooth, damp skin. Fish have fins and gills. Which ones are amphibians?
practice.explain: Only the frogs are amphibians, so the answer is {a}. The {b} fish are in the fish group.

practice.prompt: A bat can fly. Which group is it in?
practice.hint: Does a bat have fur or feathers?
practice.explain: A bat has fur and feeds its babies milk, so it is a mammal. Flying does not make an animal a bird.

practice.prompt: Which clue tells a shark from a dolphin?
choices: They both live in the sea
practice.hint: A good clue is true for one animal and not the other.
practice.explain: Dolphin babies drink milk, so a dolphin is a mammal. A shark is a fish. Fins and the sea are true of both.

pool.prompt: At the farm there are {a} cows and {b} hens. How many of them are mammals?
pool.hint: Cows have hair and feed their calves milk. Hens have feathers.
pool.explain: The {a} cows are mammals. The {b} hens have feathers, so they are birds. The answer is {a}.

pool.prompt: A zoo has {a} snakes, {b} crocodiles and 4 penguins. How many reptiles are there?
pool.hint: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin. Penguins have feathers.
pool.explain: Snakes and crocodiles are reptiles: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. Penguins are birds, so they do not count.

pool.hint: A frog is an amphibian. Think of how it feels.
pool.explain: A frog has smooth, damp skin. That is what makes it an amphibian. Dry scales are for reptiles.

pool.prompt: Mo says a whale is a fish because it lives in the sea. What is true?
choices: A whale is a mammal: it breathes air and its babies drink milk
Mo is right, it is a fish
pool.hint: Is it where the animal lives, or its body, that tells you the group?
pool.explain: A whale breathes air and feeds its babies milk, so it is a mammal. Living in the sea does not make an animal a fish.

pool.prompt: Which one is the odd one out? Eagle, bat, penguin.
pool.hint: Two have feathers. One has fur.
pool.explain: The bat has fur, so it is a mammal. The eagle and the penguin have feathers: they are birds.
A tortoise has dry scales, so it is a reptile. A toad is an amphibian and a trout is a fish.

choices: No, a penguin is a bird but it cannot fly
No, birds that cannot fly are fish
pool.hint: What makes a bird a bird: flying, or feathers and a beak?
pool.explain: A penguin cannot fly, but it has feathers and a beak, so it is still a bird.
